common_name: Millennia Blueberry (Early-Midseason University of Florida Southern Highbush Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in winter in strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark; Millennia is a vigorous University of Florida southern highbush release with a moderate chilling requirement suited to the mild, erratic winters of the Gulf Coast.

directions: Millennia is a University of Florida southern highbush release from the Lyrene breeding program, first released in 2001 and since become one of the most widely planted low-chill blueberry cultivars in north-central Florida. The vigorous, upright bush blooms and ripens in the early-to-midseason window and carries a moderate chilling requirement for a southern highbush selection, letting it perform reliably through the mild, unpredictable winters typical of the Gulf Coast. Plant alongside another southern highbush cultivar with an overlapping bloom period to improve fruit set and berry size. Prune out the oldest canes each winter and keep the shallow root zone mulched with pine bark to conserve moisture through the humid growing season.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Southern Highbush Blueberry Cultivars (HS1245)

common_name: Endura Blueberry (Late-Season Firm-Fruited University of Florida Southern Highbush Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in winter in strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark; Endura is a low-chill University of Florida southern highbush release from 2015 bred to extend the Gulf Coast harvest into the late season.

directions: Endura is a low-chill southern highbush blueberry released by the University of Florida in 2015, bred to extend the Gulf Coast harvest window into the late season. Its berries are notably large and firm with an excellent, persistent blue color that holds up well to handling and short-term storage, making it a strong choice for growers who want fruit that survives the walk from bush to kitchen. The upright, vigorous bush carries a somewhat higher chilling requirement than the earliest-ripening Florida releases, so it performs best where winters reliably deliver at least a moderate chill accumulation. Grow alongside another late-season southern highbush cultivar for best cross-pollination and berry size.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Southern Highbush Blueberry Cultivars (HS1245)

common_name: Sentinel Blueberry (Vigorous Early-Season University of Florida Southern Highbush Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in winter in strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark; Sentinel, approved for release by the University of Florida in 2020, is a vigorous early-season selection with good natural leafing that typically does not require hydrogen cyanamide defoliation sprays.

directions: Sentinel is a vigorous, high-yielding southern highbush blueberry approved for release by the University of Florida in 2020 and bred for early-season production with no known significant disease issues. Its firm berries have scored well above older standard varieties like Emerald in consumer taste panels, and the bush's naturally good leafing habit means it typically does not require hydrogen cyanamide defoliation sprays to break dormancy evenly, simplifying management for home growers. The upright, productive plant suits both hand harvest and mechanical picking and has performed consistently across Florida growing regions. Provide highly acidic, well-drained soil and pair with another early-season southern highbush cultivar for best pollination.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Southern Highbush Blueberry Cultivars (HS1245)

common_name: Contorta Jujube (Dragon Jujube, Contorted Twisted-Branch Jujube)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than most fruit trees once established, and Contorta's dramatically twisted branching gives it added value as a winter architectural specimen.

directions: Contorta, sometimes sold as Dragon Jujube, is an ornamental selection of the common Chinese jujube prized for its exaggerated, tightly zigzagging and twisted branch structure, which gives even young trees striking winter architectural interest reminiscent of a corkscrew hazel. Like all jujubes it tolerates heat, drought, and poor or alkaline soils far better than most fruit trees once established, and it thrives in the long, hot summers of the Gulf Coast. Fruit is edible and has the typical apple-crisp texture and sweetness of jujube when harvested at the tan-mottled stage, though yields and fruit size are generally smaller than on fruiting-focused cultivars like Li or Sherwood since Contorta is grown primarily for its ornamental branch form. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; a second jujube cultivar nearby improves fruit set, though established trees will still produce some fruit on their own.
